issue: Must the government plead and prove a defendant's non-Indian status as an element of an 18 U.S.C. § 1152 offense, or is the defendant's Indian status an affirmative defense that the defendant must first raise?

sides.position: Non-Indian status is an affirmative defense: the government need not allege or prove it in the indictment, and the defendant must first properly raise Indian status, after which the government bears the ultimate burden of proof.
cases: United States v. Hester, 719 F.2d 1038 (9th Cir. 1983)
United States v. Haggerty, 997 F.3d 292 (5th Cir. 2021)

sides.position: Non-Indian status is an element of the § 1152 offense that the government must plead and prove at trial.
cases: United States v. Prentiss, 256 F.3d 971 (10th Cir. 2001) (en banc)
United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)

this_court: Non-Indian status is an element the government must prove, following Prentiss; the court declines to revisit Prentiss and says it must abide by existing precedent unless and until the court reconsiders it en banc.
quote: Circuits have split on the question whether the Indian or non-Indian status of the defendant must be pleaded and proved by the government in a prosecution under 18 U.S.C.A. § 1152.
cite: United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)
